output:
Short answer: pick an adjustable LED task/desk lamp (not halogen/incandescent) with high efficacy, dimming, and a good CRI. Prefer a lamp that’s ENERGY STAR or DLC listed, 500–1,200 lumens (depending on how bright you want), color temperature ~3000–4000 K for general office tasks, and power draw in the ~5–15 W range.

Why this recommendation (evidence)
- LEDs are far more efficient than incandescent/halogen (much higher lumens per watt), so for the same usable light they use far less electricity. (This is a long-established efficiency fact used by DOE/ENERGY STAR guidance.)
- ENERGY STAR / DesignLights Consortium (DLC) listings indicate independent performance testing for efficacy, lumen maintenance and safety — good proxies for “energy-efficient” in a commercial/office context.
- Lumens and beam control matter more than wattage alone: task lighting should deliver adequate illuminance at the work surface. Choosing a lamp by lumen output and beam/spread ensures usable light while avoiding wasted output.
- CRI (color rendering index) ≥ 80–90 improves readability and color fidelity; offices typically benefit from CRI ≥ 80, professional work may prefer CRI ≥ 90.
- Dimming and occupancy controls reduce on-time and let you lower power draw when full brightness is not needed.
- Adjustable arms and glare/shade design reduce the need for higher power output (you can direct less light exactly where needed).

Practical targets to use when comparing models
- Lumens: ~500–1,200 lm depending on preference. (500 lm = modest task lighting; 1,000+ lm = very bright.)
- Power: ~5–15 W for LED desk lamps that produce the lumen ranges above (confirm actual lm/W on the spec sheet).
- Efficacy: look for listed lm/W; higher is better. Many good LED lamps are 80–120+ lm/W.
- Color temperature: 3000–4000 K for typical office (warm-neutral to neutral white). Choose cooler temps only if you prefer a daylight look.
- CRI: ≥ 80, preferably ≥ 90 for color-critical tasks.
- Certifications: ENERGY STAR or DLC preferred.
- Controls: stepless dimming, multiple brightness steps, and optional motion sensor/timer or smart control (if you want centralized lighting/automation).

Claims you should verify on a product page (don’t assume)
- Actual lumen output and lumens-per-watt (lm/W). Marketing sometimes quotes “equivalent wattage” instead of real lumen figures.
- ENERGY STAR or DLC listing — check the certifier’s database or the product spec page for the certification ID.
- Specified CRI and color temperature (Kelvin).
- Whether dimming is smooth and what dimmer types are supported (some LEDs only dim with compatible drivers).
- Warranty and rated lifetime (e.g., L70 at 50,000 hours).
- Measured power draw at different brightness settings (to confirm energy savings).
- Compatibility with smart-home or office lighting systems, if required.

Catalog note and next steps
- I checked our product catalog and found entries for desk lamps, task lamps, and adjustable desk lamps (I can pull specific SKUs and side-by-side comparisons). Tell me:
  - Desired brightness (subtle/ambient vs very bright task light)
  - Style (minimal clamp/mount, freestanding, swing-arm)
  - Budget range
  - Want ENERGY STAR/DLC only?
  - Need smart controls or USB charging?

If you tell me those, I’ll fetch and compare specific catalog models (showing specs and which claims need independent verification).
